**Airbnb Terms of Service Summary**

The service is called the Airbnb Terms of Service, which governs your relationship with Airbnb and applies to the products and services described on their official terms page.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope**: These terms cover all interactions between you and Airbnb.
* **Content and License**: You grant Airbnb a license to use your submitted content to operate, improve, and train their AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy**: The terms refer to Airbnb's published Privacy Policy, which outlines how they collect and process your personal data.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Most terms require you to participate in binding arbitration, which means going to private dispute resolution instead of court. There is a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.
* **Termination**: Either party can terminate the agreement under the conditions stated in the live document.

**Harmful Clauses to Notice:**

* **Mandatory Arbitration**: As mentioned earlier, most terms require binding arbitration, which can limit your options and potentially make it harder to seek justice.
* **Class-Action Waivers**: You may also be unable to participate in class-action lawsuits, which can make it harder to join collective legal actions.

Please keep in mind that this summary is not a substitute for reading the full Terms of Service document. It's essential to review the document for yourself and address any concerns or questions you may have. If you're unsure about any of these points or would like to opt out of arbitration, please refer to the provided opt-out window in the document.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — AIRBNB TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Airbnb and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added new AnyWhere/Icons experience terms, revised cancellation and refund policies (including AirCover updates), added language on automated/AI-driven listing detection (e.g. anti-party tools), and updated arbitration provisions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Airbnb to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 .

**Service Name:** Cloudflare Self-Serve Subscription Agreement

**Key Provisions:**

* These terms govern your relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services listed on their official terms page.
* **Changes from the previous version:** Cloudflare improved terms related to AI Gateway and Workers AI, made it clear user prompts and outputs aren't used to train Cloudflare's models, and strengthened rules to prevent scraping and AI-bot abuse.
* **Content and Licensing:** Cloudflare uses user-submitted content to operate and improve its services, including AI and machine learning systems, subject to your settings and applicable laws.
* **Privacy:** Your personal data will be governed by Cloudflare's [published Privacy Policy](https://www.cloudflare.com/privacy-policy/) which explains categories of information collected and how it is processed.
* **Dispute Resolution:** Cloudflare usually requires **binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court)** with **class-action waivers (limiting the ability to join lawsuits with others)**, except for **Steam accounts**. You have a 30-day window to opt-out and avoid binding arbitration when opening a new account.
* **Termination:** Either Cloudflare or you can end this agreement according to the live document.
* **Contact:** For concerns about these terms, please visit [https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/](https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/) for more information.

**Flags of Concern:**

The **binding arbitration and class-action waiver** provisions in Dispute Resolution may limit your ability to resolve disputes in court or join class-action lawsuits. This means you might not have the right to participate in collective actions against Cloudflare.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — CLOUDFLARE SELF-SERVE SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Cloudflare to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ .

**Summary of Stripe Services Agreement (US)**

The Terms of Service governing this agreement are the Stripe Services Agreement (US), effective 2024.

**Key Provisions:**

- **Scope:** These terms cover your relationship with Stripe and apply to the various products and services listed on their official terms page.
- **Content and License:** Stripe can use your submitted content to operate, improve, and train its AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
- **Privacy:** The terms link to Stripe's published Privacy Policy, which outlines personal data categories and processing practices.
- **Dispute Resolution:** Most terms require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, but you can opt out within 30 days of creating an account. Notable exceptions include Steam (Valve), which has removed mandatory arbitration.
- **Termination:** Either party can terminate the agreement based on conditions outlined in the live document.

**Concerning Clauses:**

- **Arbitration:** Requiring binding arbitration with class-action waivers may limit users' ability to join class actions and negotiate settlements. However, you can opt out within 30 days of creating an account.
- **Loss of IP Rights:** Although it's not explicitly mentioned, the **Content and License** clause might imply that Stripe can use your content without obtaining separate permission or compensating you. Consider this limitation when submitting content to Stripe.

Remember, these terms serve as a binding agreement between Stripe and you, their user. While it's essential to review and understand them, the detailed content and conditions should be consulted directly within the provided URL.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STRIPE SERVICES AGREEMENT (US) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stripe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised Connect platform-onboarding obligations, added Stripe Radar/AI-fraud-prevention provisions, refreshed dispute and chargeback handling sections, and updated indemnification and liability caps.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stripe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stripe.com/legal/ssa .

The Terms of Service are for Shopify, a platform for online stores. 

Here's a summary of the key provisions:

* **Scope**: These terms apply to your relationship with Shopify and cover the services they provide.
* **Content and License**: When you submit content to Shopify, they might use it to improve their AI systems. This might happen even if you're not actively using those features.
* **Privacy**: Shopify's Privacy Policy explains what personal data they collect and how they process it. The Terms of Service point to this policy, but don't include the details here.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Most users must use binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) to resolve disputes. You have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts. Note that this is a change from the normal opt-out process, which typically requires action within a relatively short time frame (and so might be hard to fulfill, if not remembered and acted upon).
* **Termination**: Either you or Shopify can terminate the agreement. Conditions apply, but they're not outlined here.
* **Contact**: If you have questions, check Shopify's published contact information on their website.

Potential issues to watch out for:

* Binding arbitration (dispute resolution) might not give you a chance to have a case heard in court if the other party doesn't agree with you.
* The Terms of Service give Shopify some flexibility with using your content for AI-related features, which might be hard to predict or control.
* Payouts and risk-scoring sections have been revised, so it's worth taking a closer look at those to understand any changes.

That's a general summary of the Terms of Service for Shopify. If you have specific questions, feel free to ask.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SHOPIFY TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Shopify and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions, clarified that merchant store content may be used to power AI features only at the merchant's store level (not for training shared models), and revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Shopify to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms .

**Service Name:** Wikimedia Terms of Use (also known as the Terms of Service)

The Wikimedia Terms of Use are the rules that govern your relationship with Wikipedia (managed by Wikimedia Foundation) and apply to its various products and services.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope**: These terms apply to Wikipedia and its services as listed on the official terms page.
* **Content and License**: When you submit content, Wikipedia uses it to operate, improve, and train its AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy**: The terms reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which explains the categories of personal data collected and how it's processed.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Most terms require binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) with class-action waivers. However, you have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.
* **Termination**: Either party can terminate the agreement subject to certain conditions.

**Potentially Harmful Clauses:**

* **Dispute Resolution**: Requiring binding arbitration and class-action waivers can limit your ability to seek redress through the courts. However, you have a 30-day opt-out window.
* **Content and License**: The terms allow Wikipedia to use your user-submitted content in various ways, including training AI/ML systems. While this is standard practice, it may raise concerns about data ownership and control.
* **Termination**: The terms do not specify the exact conditions for terminating the agreement, which may lead to uncertainty or disputes.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — WIKIMEDIA TERMS OF USE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2014 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2014 version in the following ways: Effective June 7, 2023: first major rewrite since 2014. Added Universal Code of Conduct as binding, updated paid-contributions disclosure rules, modernized account-security and dispute-resolution provisions, and added explicit language covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use . The previous version is available at https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use/9_June_2014 .

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- - The time period for retaining account data after account deletion has increased from 18 months to 36 months.
- - You no longer have the right to participate in class actions when disputes are resolved by binding arbitration.
- - The license granted to ChirpSocial for content you post is no longer limited in time and is now perpetual and irrevocable.
- - The content license may be used for advertising, whereas previously it was unclear what uses it could be put to.
- - ChirpSocial no longer sends an email to registered users before making material changes to the Terms; instead, you are considered to have accepted any changes by continuing to use the service.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's take a look at the changes.

The most significant change is in the DATA RETENTION policy. Previously, ChirpSocial retained your account data for 18 months after you deleted your account. Now, they retain it for 36 months. This means your data will be stored by ChirpSocial for a longer period.

Another change is related to the CONTENT LICENSE. Under the previous version, ChirpSocial had the right to display your content. Now, they have a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from any content you post, which includes using it for advertising. This is a broader license than before, and you should be aware of the potential commercial uses of your content.

Lastly, the CHANGES clause has been updated. Previously, ChirpSocial would send you an email 30 days before any material change to the Terms. Now, by continuing to use the service, you are considered to have accepted any changes made to the Terms.

It's also worth noting that the ARBITRATION clause has been updated. Under the previous version, you had the right to participate in class actions, even if disputes are resolved by binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court). Now, this right is waived.

New clauses or significant updates:

* DATA RETENTION: retaining account data for 36 months after account deletion (could potentially harm you if sensitive information is stored)
* CONTENT LICENSE: license is worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, and royalty-free, allowing commercial use (could potentially harm you financially)
* ARBITRATION: class actions are waived (could potentially harm you by limiting your access to group lawsuits)

Please note that these have been introduced in the new Terms of Service, and it's essential to be aware of them.
source_tos:
1. ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from content you post, including for advertising.
3. DATA RETENTION. We retain account data for 36 months after account deletion.
4. ARBITRATION. Disputes are resolved by binding arbitration. You waive the right to participate in any class action.
5. CHANGES. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use constitutes acceptance.

[MATERIAL CHANGES]
- Content license expanded from display-only royalty-free to perpetual, irrevocable, including modification, derivative works, and advertising use.
- Data retention after deletion increased from 18 months to 36 months.
- Arbitration clause now adds a class-action waiver (previously not waived).
- Change-of-terms notice removed: previously 30 days' email notice required, now changes take effect via continued use without notice.
[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Section 1 wording is identical.

substantial

Under PURCHASES, the timeframe for all sales to be final has been shortened from 14 days to 7 days after delivery.

Under RETURNS, the most significant change is that you're no longer eligible for a full refund. If you want to return an item, you can only get store credit, which you have up to 14 days to do. Previously, you had the same 14 days to get a full refund.

Additionally, the refund eligibility duration is now shorter and ends 7 days after delivery (not 14).

Payment options have been expanded to include a new method called ShopFast Pay, but the others remain the same.

When it comes to PRIVACY, the way we share your purchase history has changed. Previously, you could opt out of this sharing unless you explicitly chose in. Now, it's more complicated – you can only opt out if you're a user based in the European Union (EU), not if you're outside that area.

The Terms of Service do not address concerns about your rights or potential limitations on store credit, so I'm highlighting the return policy changes: 
- You will receive store credit instead of a refund when returning an item.
- You have a shorter window (7 days) to dispute purchases before they become final.

Be sure to review the Privacy section if you're not in the EU.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Google's license to use uploaded content is broadened to include operating, developing, and improving its services, including AI services.
- A new restriction is imposed on users regarding the use of Google's generative-AI features, prohibitinig abuse, reverse-engineering, or extraction of underlying models.
- The content of the dispute-resolution and governing-law sections have been updated, but specific details are not provided.
- The warranty disclaimers and capped-liability language have been updated in the NEW VERSION, but specific changes are not detailed.

[NARRATIVE]
To help you understand the changes, let's go through the updates:

* The license to use your uploaded content has been broadened. This means that previously, Google could only host, reproduce, and display your content to operate the services. Now, the license also includes using your content to operate, develop, and improve its services, including its AI services.
* A new restriction has been added, specifically for Google's generative-AI features. You are no longer allowed to abuse, reverse-engineer, or attempt to extract the underlying models from these features. This could be a concern if you were using these features to try and understand their inner workings.

No new clauses have been explicitly flagged as "harmful" in the provided reference text; these are just the changes. The Terms of Service is a legal document, so I would advise you to review it thoroughly when reading the new and updated provisions.

The changes to the dispute-resolution and governing-law sections are mentioned, but specific details are not provided. It's also worth noting that the warranty disclaimers and capped-liability language have been updated, but the specific changes are not detailed in the summary.

1. SCOPE. These Terms cover your use of Google services and reorganize prior provisions into clearer sections.

3. AI. New section: users may not abuse, reverse-engineer, or attempt to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features.
4. DISPUTES. Updated dispute-resolution and governing-law sections.
5. LIABILITY. Updated warranty disclaimers and capped-liability language.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The effective date of this Terms of Service document moved from 2024 to 2025.
- Users can now know which data they can export, as this information was added.
- Some external factors may govern the separate support terms for certain services.
- Trial offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on.
- Non-Microsoft third-party platforms are allowed to track and share user data when using Xbox Game Studio titles.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to clarify and expand on some points, but they also introduce some changes. 

One notable change is that the effective date of this Terms of Service document is now 2025. 

There are a few new clauses to note:

* In the 'YOUR CONTENT' section, there is now a subsection on exportable data. This explicitly details what data users can take with them. This is generally a positive addition as it provides more transparency.
* In the 'SUPPORT' section, it is now stated that some services may have separate support terms governed outside this agreement. This means you may not be subject to the standard support terms, but the specifics will depend on the external governing terms.
* In the 'PAYMENT' section, it is clarified that some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on. Before, the Terms only mentioned the conversion of trial offers, but now it explicitly mentions the auto-renewal part. This can be a potential issue if you're not paying close attention to your subscriptions.
* In the 'XBOX' section, it is now mentioned that non-Microsoft third-party platforms are allowed to track and share user data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles. This expands on the previous terms, but it might be concerning for users who value their data privacy.

The changes to these terms aim to provide more clarity and transparency.

4. PAYMENT. Adds language clarifying that some trial-period offers may require auto-renewal to be turned on.
5. XBOX. Adds language about non-Microsoft third-party platforms tracking and sharing user data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The moderation rules are now supplemented with an external link to a Microsoft policy page for more detailed information.
- The service will track and share user data hosted on third-party platforms, subject to those platforms' terms.
- The availability of family-settings features may be limited or not available on third-party platforms.
- The service's effective date has been updated from 2023 to 2024.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated from the 2023 version to the 2024 version. Several changes are worth noting:

* **Effective Date**: The effective date of the Terms of Service has changed from 2023 to 2024. (This change is mostly a marker that the terms are current, but it doesn't directly affect your use of Microsoft services.)
* **Moderation**: The moderation rules are now supplemented with a link to an external Microsoft policy page for more detailed information (2).
* **Xbox**: The 2024 version adds a disclosure that third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data, subject to those platforms' terms (3). **This change may harm you if you're not aware that third-party platforms are collecting your data.**
* **Kids on Xbox**: The 2024 version clarifies that family-settings features may not be available on third-party platforms (4). **This change may harm you if your child uses Xbox on a third-party platform and you need to control their online experience.**

These changes aim to highlight the external moderation policy and the potential data collection on third-party Xbox platforms, and adjust some of the rules related to Xbox's kid-friendly features. As always, it's essential to review and understand the updated Terms of Service to avoid any potential issues.

There doesn't appear to be any explicit clauses in the new version that directly harm you. However, it's natural to be cautious when changes are made to the Terms of Service.

*   **Changes in arbitration**: A change in arbitration providers might imply that the procedure and costs associated with it could be different.

Regarding indemnification, the language has been updated, consolidating the provision into the new agreement. This updated provision takes effect from this version.

Additionally, service-level commitments have been consolidated and updated. However, this version does not provide information about specific changes, so their impact is unclear.

* The Acceptable Use Policy section has been strengthened. The new version now directly references the published policy instead of just mentioning a separate document. This means you should read the policy carefully to understand what's expected of you.

However, without more information, it's unclear how this would specifically harm you.

As for additional clauses, I didn't find any new provisions that could be considered particularly onerous. However, I did note that the dispute resolution section was updated, but the changes aren't explicitly stated.

Overall, the changes seem to bring about more explicit language and clearer communication in certain areas, but it's essential to carefully review the updated Terms of Service to ensure you're comfortable with the changes.

The **CUSTOMER DATA** section has been updated with expanded provisions on customer data and outputs. This change provides more clarity on how your data is handled.

Additionally, the **TRAINING** section has been updated to explicitly state that customer prompts and completions are not used to train Anthropic models by default. This means that without your explicit consent, your data won't be used to train the models.

Lastly, the **INDEMNIFICATION** section has been revised. This change ties indemnification and acceptable-use language to the published Usage Policy. 

There aren't any new clauses that specifically harm users. However, a crucial point to note is that training on your customer data is no longer used by default. If you wish to benefit from this, you might need to opt-in specifically.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope of the license has been expanded to include use, distribution, and modification of uploaded content.
- You are now granting a more explicit permission for Meta to use and process your content across all Meta Products for service operation and improvement.
- There is now a more detailed and explicit clause for data flow across Meta Products like Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger.
- The Content License now includes the right for Meta to modify your uploaded content.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service say that the scope of the license has been expanded. Previously, it covered only hosting and displaying your content (previous clause 2). Now, it includes use, distribution, and modification of uploaded content (current clause 2 and change summary). This expanded license gives Meta more flexibility to use your content.

Another change is the introduction of AI/ML processing of content across Meta Products for service operation and improvement. This was not mentioned in the previous Terms of Service. Meta is now allowed to use and process your content in this new way (current clause 3 and change summary).

The Terms of Service also now explicitly mention that your content might be modified by Meta. This is mentioned in the change summary.

Lastly, the data flow across Meta Products has been detailed and made more explicit. Meta now discusses flowing your data across Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger (current clause 4 and change summary).

As for potential harm, I'd like to highlight a few new points that may be worth considering:

* The expanded license allows Meta to modify your content without notifying you.
* Meta is now allowed to process your content using AI/ML technologies, which could potentially affect copyright or intellectual property issues.

Keep in mind that these changes only reflect what the Terms of Service say. If you're unsure about the implications, you may want to consult with a legal expert for personalized advice.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- CONTRACTING PARTY changed from TikTok Inc. to TikTok USDS.
- CONTENT LICENSE becomes irrevocable and reaffirmed for ML model development.
- New generative-AI rules added, including 'outputs are as is' and increased user responsibility for inputs/outputs.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. 

Firstly, the contracting party has changed from TikTok Inc. to TikTok USDS, which is "the U.S. joint venture". This change in contracting party does not affect your usage of the platform, but it clarifies the entity responsible for any agreements.

Next, the content license has been updated. Previously, it was a worldwide royalty-free sublicensable license over user content. Now, it's the same worldwide license, irrevocable, royalty-free, and sublicensable. In addition, the new version reaffirms this license for machine learning (ML) model development. While this reaffirmation may provide some benefits, it also means the license will now be irrevocable, which means you won't be able to cancel it even if circumstances change.

You may want to be cautious with the new generative-AI rules. Since outputs are now 'as is', you won't be able to rely on them being perfect or perfectible. Also, users are now held responsible for both the inputs and outputs of AI generated content. This means if the AI generates content that's problematic, you may be held accountable. Furthermore, users are prohibited from stripping watermarks from AI output or claiming AI-generated content is human-made.

Here are some key changes:
* **Increased contract permanence**: The content license is now **irrevocable**.
* **New AI-related responsibilities**: Users are now **responsible for inputs and outputs of AI-generated content**.
* **Additional restrictions on AI-generated content**: You may not **strip watermarks** or **claim AI output is human-made**.

Be aware that these new clauses and changes may have implications for how you use the platform, especially when it comes to AI-generated content. Make sure you understand the changes before continuing to use the service.

1. CONTRACTING PARTY. TikTok USDS (after the U.S. joint venture).
2. CONTENT LICENSE. Same worldwide, irrevocable, royalty-free, sublicensable license, reaffirmed for ML model development.
3. AGE. Reaffirmed: users under 13 use the Under-13 Experience.
4. AI. New generative-AI rules: outputs are 'as is'; users are responsible for inputs/outputs; users may not strip watermarks or claim AI output is human-made.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- YouTube now has the right to monetize non-partner creators' videos.
- There is an explicit prohibition on collecting facial-recognition data from videos.
- Non-U.S. creators who receive payments have new U.S. tax-withholding obligations.
- The Terms now apply globally, rather than being region-specific.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the key changes.

Firstly, the right to monetize videos has been expanded. Previous to this change, only creators who joined the YouTube Partner Program (YPP) could **monetize their videos**. Now, **most videos on the platform can be monetized**, including those of non-partner creators. 

Regarding **facial recognition**, there is an explicit prohibition on collecting facial-recognition data from videos. This means you can't use the platform to collect or share other users' facial information.

We also see a change in tax obligations for creators. Non-U.S. creators who receive payments from YouTube now have **U.S. tax-withholding obligations**. This is a new tax rule that might affect some creators.

Additionally, the Terms of Service have been **globalized**, which means the same rules now apply worldwide, not just in specific regions.

In terms of potential harm, the new tax responsibilities specifically for non-U.S. creators might be burdensome.

2. FACIAL RECOGNITION. Explicit prohibition on collecting facial-recognition data from videos.

4. SCOPE. Globalized version of the Terms.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Zoom now has a broad license to use service-generated data to train AI/ML models (previously no specific restriction).
- Zoom will train AI models using customer audio, video, and chat content only after obtaining customer consent (previously permitted).
- The use of customer audio/video/chat is now subject to customer-controlled settings (previously covered by general privacy commitments).

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'll guide you through the key changes. 

Zoom now has a broad license to use service-generated data (data created by the Zoom service, like usage metrics) to train artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models. This means Zoom can use data like how often you use the service and what features you use most, but not actual customer content like audio or video recordings, without needing your explicit permission to do so.

On the other hand, there's been a significant change regarding how Zoom uses AI training with customer content. Previously, there was no specific clause about AI training, but now after public backlash in August 2023, Zoom explicitly states that it won't train AI models with customer content (like audio, video, or chat) without your consent.

The use of customer audio, video, and chat content is now subject to your control through customer-controlled settings. This implies you decide how the data is used, which is an improvement from the previous policy where it was only governed by general privacy commitments.

In these updates, one major addition is that March 2023 update gave Zoom broad service-generated data license. This was previously under Standard provisions on Zoom's use of telemetry and operational data, which is the least invasive usage we now know with the updates.

Key changes:

* Zoom can now use all service-generated data to train AI and ML models, without your permission
* Zoom will ask for your consent before training AI models using your customer content (audio, video, or chat)
* You have more control over how your customer content is used (you control the settings)
source_tos:
1. SERVICE-GENERATED DATA. March 2023 update added a broad license over Service-Generated Data permitting Zoom to use it to train AI/ML models.
2. AI TRAINING. After backlash in August 2023, Zoom amended the Terms to expressly state that audio, video, and chat content are not used to train AI models without customer consent.
3. CUSTOMER CONTENT. Customer audio/video/chat continues to be subject to customer-controlled use.

1. SERVICE-GENERATED DATA. Standard provisions on Zoom's use of telemetry and operational data.
2. AI TRAINING. No specific AI-training clause.
3. CUSTOMER CONTENT. Customer audio/video/chat covered by privacy commitments.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The NEW version explicitly allows the use of user data and content for AI training, in addition to other standard uses.
- The NEW version introduces a new opt-out feature to prevent AI training from user data and content.
- The NEW version includes a clause that waives class-action lawsuits, whereas the OLD version allowed for arbitration and class-action lawsuits.
- The NEW version explicitly states that user data and content may be used to train "generative-AI" models, which is not mentioned in the OLD version.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's compare the old and new versions of the Terms of Service. 

The new version explicitly allows the use of your data and content for AI training (1), including training generative-AI models for LinkedIn features. Previously, the policy was vague about AI training, but now it's explicitly stated that LinkedIn can use your data and content for this purpose.

The new version introduces a new opt-out toggle in your Settings (3) to prevent LinkedIn from training AI models using your data and content. This means you now have a choice whether to allow your data to be used for AI training.

The dispute-resolution provisions have been updated (4). The old version allowed for both arbitration and class-action lawsuits, while the new version includes a class-action waiver language. This means you'll have to resolve disputes individually through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) rather than being part of a group lawsuit.

In terms of potential harms, the new class-action waiver might limit your ability to join a group lawsuit against LinkedIn. However, you can review your Settings to opt-out of AI training, which should prevent LinkedIn from using your data in this way.

Here are key changes:

* New opt-out feature to prevent AI training from user data and content
* Class-action lawsuit waiver in dispute-resolution provisions

4. DISPUTES. Updated dispute-resolution provisions, including class-action waiver language.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version allowed using customer data to train Slack's global model, 
  whereas the NEW version does not use customer data to train generative-AI products.
- The NEW version narrows the scope of using customer data for global model training 
  from the OLD version.
- New Slack-AI-specific terms have been added to the NEW version.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'll walk you through the changes. 

Three main changes have occurred. 

* Previously, the policy was unclear about how customer data is used. Now, customer data is specifically clarified to not be used to train Slack's generative-AI products. 
* Earlier, the private-policy language about ML use for global model training was broad. This version narrows that language, which may mean less customer data is being used for model training than before.
* New Slack-AI-specific terms have been added. This is a new addition and may impact how your data is handled, but I'll need more information about these terms to determine any potential risks.

In terms of potential harm, the one area to watch is the clarification that customer data is not used to train Slack's generative-AI products. If something changes and it is used for that, we will revisit this. 

It is worth noting AI and generative-AI products are complex areas.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The data-export limits for apps are now clarified.
- The restrictions on bulk extraction by apps are being made stricter.
- You are now required to get permission before using Slack data to train large language models.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's walk through the changes. 

The Terms of Service have clarified some points and added restrictions. Here are the key changes:

* Clarification on data-export limits (APP DATA): The new version of the Terms of Service is more specific about the data that apps can export. However, it doesn't necessarily change the rules, but rather clarifies them.
* Stricter restrictions on bulk extraction by apps (BULK EXTRACTION): The new version makes it stricter for apps to extract data in bulk.
* New explicit prohibition on using Slack data to train large language models (LLM USE): The new Terms of Service specifically state that you need permission from Slack to use their data to train large language models.

These changes seem focused on protecting user data and preventing unauthorized uses. However, if you're using Slack data to train large language models (LLMs) without permission, this new clause adds a specific prohibition. If you're interested in using Slack data for this purpose, you should contact Slack to discuss what you need to do to get permission.

Note that the new clauses don't mention any specific penalties for non-compliance, but they do make it mandatory for you to obtain permission if you want to use Slack data for training LLMs. 

If you use Slack's API, be aware that you will need to follow these new stricter rules, especially regarding bulk extraction. Make sure to review the updated APP DATA and BULK EXTRACTION sections to understand your responsibilities.

  * The Terms of Service now require users to give proper credit and attribution when using AI-generated content.
  The added rules about AI-generated content are new and you might need to pay attention to these changes.

* **Paid Services**: The Paid Service Terms have been expanded to be more clear and specific.
   These updates focus mostly on making it easier to understand the terms and conditions that apply to paid services.
   So you can expect to see more refined description of what you can and can't do with Paid Services.
* **Safety Metadata**: This version adds that metadata from safety features may be used to train safety systems.
   This means that any data you submit for safety reasons will be used to teach algorithms how to identify similar safety issues in the future.

There is no new language in the updated Terms of Service that would give me cause for concern.
However, the introduction of AI-generated content rules and the use of metadata for safety systems are items that you may want to be aware of in order to ensure compliance.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Personal data may now be shared with Microsoft, which was not previously mentioned.
- Personal data is now shared with affiliates for AI/ML model development.
- Data is now explicitly processed for AI/ML model training.
- User data protections no longer apply when shared with affiliates.
- User opt-out preferences no longer remain applicable with affiliates.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service say that personal data can now be shared with GitHub's affiliates for AI/ML model development. This is a new purpose for sharing data, which wasn't covered in the previous policy.

Previously, personal data was only shared with affiliates for limited operational purposes, whereas now you can expect your data to be used for training AI/ML models. Here are some of the key changes:

* Personal data is now shared for AI/ML model development with affiliates like Microsoft.
* Data is processed for new purposes, including AI/ML model training, which wasn't specified before.
* When data is shared with affiliates, your opt-out preferences may not travel with the data, meaning your protections might not apply in this scenario.
 

These changes directly affect clauses 2 of PROCESSING PURPOSES and 4 of OPT-OUTS.

1. AFFILIATES. Personal data may now be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development.
2. PROCESSING PURPOSES. New product-development purpose explicitly covering AI/ML model training.
3. AI/ML. Explicit purpose for using personal data to develop, improve, and train AI/ML models.
4. OPT-OUTS. User opt-out preferences and enterprise data protections travel with the data when shared with affiliates.

There is a new clause regarding monetization, which means that Reddit may have more control over how ads are displayed and revenue is generated on the platform. 

Additionally, the dispute-resolution venue has been changed. This refers to the platform or process that will be used to resolve disputes between you and Reddit.

As for clauses that may potentially harm you, I want to highlight the issue with user content being licensed to third parties for AI training. You may be concerned about your personal data and how it's being used. 

Here are some points to consider:

* Your content is now licensed to third parties, which may include AI training data.
* The Terms of Service don't explicitly state what happens to your data once it's licensed.
* AI training data is often used for machine learning purposes, which may lead to further use of your data or derivative works.

To be clear, I'm not providing any opinion on whether these changes are detrimental or not. My role is to communicate the changes and help you understand the new Terms of Service. If you're concerned, I recommend carefully reading through the Terms of Service and considering seeking independent advice.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The user-content license now covers AI processing of uploaded audio and podcasts.
- New rules have been added for AI DJ and AI-generated playlists.
- The dispute resolution process has been updated, including changes to arbitration and class-action waiver clauses.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes.

The most significant change is with **USER CONTENT**. Previously, the standard license only covered audio and podcasts uploaded by users. Now, the license has been expanded to include **AI processing of uploaded audio and podcasts**. This means that if you upload content, we can use AI to process and analyze it without needing an additional license.

Regarding **AI**, new rules have been added for **AI DJ and AI-generated playlists**. However, we don't have more information on these rules, and their impact is unclear.

Finally, the **DISPUTES** section has seen significant changes. The arbitration and class-action waiver clauses have been updated. However, the terms of arbitration remain private, and binding arbitration is a private dispute process instead of court.

There are no explicitly stated new clauses that may harm you, but the Terms of Service have expanded our rights to process your uploaded content using AI. It's essential to review the updated **USER CONTENT** clause to ensure you're comfortable with these changes.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The number of household members outside the primary household for paid sharing has been changed from "tolerated" to "requires paid additional members".
- A "Netflix Household" is now officially defined.
- The standard plan tiers and billing language have been updated to reflect the extra-member fee.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's review the updates to the Terms of Service.

* The update has changed the sharing policy. Previously, account sharing across households was **tolerated in practice**. Now, for paid sharing, you need to be part of the **primary household** and also have **paid additional members** for users outside of the household. This means that anyone outside of the primary household but still watching content on your account will need to have an additional subscription to do so.

* The term **Netflix Household** has been officially defined. However, this change doesn't have a significant impact on user rights or obligations.

* Previously, the billing and cancellation provisions were different. The Terms of Service now have updated **billing/cancellation provisions** to reflect the extra-member fee. This includes changes to the **standard plan tiers and billing language**. 

It's worth noting that there are no new clauses that directly harm users in these updates. However, users may find the updated sharing policy inconvenient if they share an account with people outside their primary household and aren't interested in adding paid memberships for them.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The "no ads" / "ad-free" tiers now may include ads.
- Arbitration procedures have been expanded with mass-arbitration procedures added.
- New and existing subscribers may have different effective dates for the Terms of Service.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated. Let's break down the changes.

The most notable change is the way ads are handled on the 'no ads' / 'ad-free' tiers. Previously, these tiers genuinely didn't have any ads during streaming. However, the updated Terms say that even on these tiers, streaming titles may include ads.

Another crucial change is the arbitration clause. Previously, standard arbitration provisions were in place, but now the arbitration procedures have been expanded to include **mass-arbitration procedures**. While the terms don't explicitly state what mass-arbitration procedures entail, it's generally a private dispute process that affects multiple users, potentially reducing your ability to seek group redress.

Lastly, the effective date for the Terms of Service has been changed. There are now different effective dates for **new** and **existing** subscribers. This means that if you're a new subscriber, the updated Terms will take effect immediately upon signing up, but if you've been an existing subscriber, you might not feel the effects of these changes right away.

These changes may harm you in a few specific ways:

* Expect ads even on the 'no ads' tier
* Mass-arbitration procedures may limit your ability to join a group lawsuit if you have a grievance
* Changes to the effective date may leave you in a situation where you're subject to the new Terms before fully understanding them

Let's walk through the changes. 

The scope of the Terms of Service has been broadened to include Alexa, Rufus AI, and other AI services. This means that these services are now covered under the same agreement as previously.

Regarding AI, the new version specifically mentions AI-generated outputs and how they interact with the user agreement. This is likely to affect use of Alexa services and Rufus AI that generates audio or content based on user requests.

Additionally, the binding arbitration clause has been updated. Previously, arbitration was mandatory for all disputes. Now, there is an explicitly carved-out exception for small-claims-court cases - these will not be subject to arbitration, allowing users to take disputes to court as they normally would (if the amount in dispute meets the local court's jurisdiction for small claims).

I do not see any changes that directly increase risk or harm to users, but the mention of AI-generated outputs does add another point to be considered: any content or audio generated through Alexa or Rufus AI should be reviewed by users to ensure it meets their expectations.

This appears to be a new protection that preserves your data and does not store it in plain text or disclose it without consent.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The CROWD-SOURCED section now applies to "Live, Local, and other crowd-sourced services", which was not explicitly mentioned before.
- The AI section has been expanded to cover "My AI and other generative-AI features", which was not mentioned before.
- A 60-day waiting period has been added to the pre-arbitration procedure.

[NARRATIVE]
This version adds a few important changes and clarifications.

The **Content License** hasn't changed, so you can expect the same standard licensing terms to apply.

A new aspect of the **Crowd-Sourced** section is that it now explicitly covers services like Live, Local, and other crowd-sourced services. This means that if you contribute to such services, your content will be subject to the same terms and conditions as the standard content.

A more significant change is the addition of new sections under **AI**, covering features like My AI and other generative-AI features. This expansion indicates that the service providers have more control over how AI technologies are used within the platform.

Another notable change is in the **Arbitration** section, which introduces a 60-day waiting period before you can proceed to binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court). This waiting period is a key part of the pre-arbitration procedure.

Now about potential harm: 

1. **Crowd-Sourced**: The expanded license terms apply not just to user content, but also to the services themselves. This means that if you contribute to Live, Local, or other crowd-sourced services, the terms may affect the way your content is used or shared.
2. **AI**: The new sections covering My AI and other generative-AI features imply that the service providers can use AI technologies to analyze and process your content in more sophisticated ways.
3. **Arbitration**: A 60-day waiting period before proceeding to arbitration can add complexity and delay to resolving disputes. This might be disadvantageous if you need to address a serious issue promptly.

* The addition of a user-facing opt-out (Settings > Visibility > Prevent third-party sharing)

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Users are now considered owners of outputs generated by Canva's AI tools, with Canva retaining certain rights.
- Canva users are no longer allowed to use Canva-generated content to train other AI models.
- AI-generated content must adhere to new content-moderation and labeling requirements.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over the updates.

The main change here is that the terms have been updated to address the use of Canva's generative-AI tools. There are three key updates to note:

* **Output ownership**: You now own the outputs generated by Canva's AI tools, but Canva retains certain platform rights. This means that while you have rights to the output, you're not completely in control of how the platform chooses to use them.
* **AI-generated content restrictions**: You're no longer allowed to use Canva-generated content to train other AI models. This is a new restriction that wasn't present in the previous terms.
* **Content-moderation and labeling requirements**: AI-generated content must adhere to new content-moderation and labeling requirements. While this may seem like a positive development, it means that Canva has more authority to moderate and label your content. 

It's worth noting that the new **AI** clause introduces specific rules for Magic Studio, which aren't present in the previous terms. However, this doesn't necessarily harm you, since it's a new clause aimed at regulating the use of Canva's AI tools.

Overall, the changes seem to be aimed at clarifying ownership and use of Canva-generated content, but they do introduce some new restrictions on how you can use your outputs.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The list of subprocessors has been updated.
- Notion has added provisions regarding input/output ownership and the training of foundational models on customer data for Notion AI.
- Enterprise plans now offer data-residency options.

[NARRATIVE]
Let me help you understand the changes. 

When it comes to **SUBPROCESSORS**, the Terms of Service have been updated to reflect a new list of subprocessors. This might not be directly impactful, but it's good to know that they've been updated to ensure compliance with their agreements. There don't seem to be any issues with this change.

Regarding **AI**, there are two key changes: 
* Notion has added provisions regarding **input/output ownership**. This means that you will retain the ownership of the data and content you input into Notion AI, but for outputs generated by the service, you should assume that Notion retains some level of ownership and rights to use the generated data.
* They've also clarified that they don't train their foundational models on your customer data by default. This means they won't use your data to improve their AI unless you opt-in.

As for **ENTERPRISE**, a new data-residency option has been introduced for Enterprise plans. This allows you to choose where your data will be stored, which might be beneficial for companies dealing with sensitive information or requiring regional compliance.

Considering these changes, the only potential clause that may require your attention is the one related to AI. Specifically, the issue with input/output ownership. The Terms of Service say that you will retain ownership of your input, but Notion may retain rights to outputs generated by the service. If you're concerned about data ownership, I recommend reviewing the section in more detail.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- In the NEW version, Figma AI features (Make Designs, Visual Search) have been added.
- In the NEW version, customer file content is not used to train third-party generative models without user opt-in, whereas previously there was no such restriction.
- The NEW version has strengthened security and incident-notification language compared to the OLD version.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service introduce a few significant changes. One key addition is the integration of Figma AI features, which include "Make Designs" and "Visual Search." 

Another update concerns customer file content. The Terms of Service now make it clear that Figma does not use customer file content to train third-party generative models unless you opt-in. This means that previously, there was no explicit prohibition against using your file content for this purpose.

The new Terms of Service also strengthen the security and incident-notification language compared to the previous version.

Looking at the changes, the new security language helps ensure that Figma maintains a high level of protection for your data. However, there's no specific clause that I can flag as potentially harming you. The changes seem to be focused on improving security and user control over their data.

2. CUSTOMER FILES. Clarified that customer file content is not used to train third-party generative models without opt-in.
3. SECURITY. Strengthened security and incident-notification language.

2. CUSTOMER FILES. Standard confidentiality language.
3. SECURITY. Standard incident-notification language.

[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Customer-file confidentiality framing existed in the prior version.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version allowed unrestricted bulk extraction for AI training, while the NEW version requires a commercial agreement for it.
- The OLD version made no mention of specific commercial AI training deals, while the NEW version explicitly mentions OpenAI and Google.
- There's a change in licensing clarity for public Q&A from the OLD being just "posted" under CC BY-SA to NEW referencing the reaffirmation of that license.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have updated the licensing agreement for public questions and answers on the Stack Overflow Public Network. Previously, the Q&A was posted under the Creative Commons License (CC BY-SA).

Now, the Terms of Service "reaffirm" the CC BY-SA licensing of public Q&A for the network. This means that the license hasn't changed, but it's been stated more clearly in the Terms of Service.

Let's move to the section on bulk use. The previous version of the Terms of Service made no specific mention of extracting content in bulk for artificial intelligence (AI) training. However, this new version adds a restriction on bulk extraction for AI training without a commercial agreement.

**New clauses of concern:**

* **Bulk use for AI training**: You may no longer extract content from the Stack Overflow Public Network in bulk for AI training without a commercial agreement. This may impact any existing projects or plans you have to use the network's content for AI training without obtaining the necessary agreement.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service mention specific commercial agreements with companies like OpenAI and Google. This could impact how you use the network's content under these agreements.

Keep in mind that the Creative Commons License (CC BY-SA) still applies to the content, which includes allowing others to share, adapt, and use the content. However, the new restriction on bulk extraction for AI training without a commercial agreement might affect how you use the network's content in this context.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope now includes Poe, in addition to the Quora Q&A platform.
- Poe-specific provisions now allow for Poe prompts/responses to be used to improve Poe and partner models, subject to user settings.
- Bot-developer terms have been added for the first time.
- Dispute-resolution provisions have been revised.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service introduce several key changes.

Firstly, the scope of the Terms now covers both Quora and Poe, whereas previously it only covered the Quora Q&A platform. This broader scope includes all Quora and Poe activities.

Secondly, the Poe-specific provisions have been expanded to include the use of Poe prompts and responses to improve Poe and partner models. While this feature may benefit some users, it's worth noting that it's subject to user settings. This means you'll have control over how your Poe activity is used in this way.

Another significant change is the addition of bot-developer terms. These are new clauses that specifically address developers working on bots (short for bots, as in automated programs - sometimes also called 'AI' or 'digital agents'). The Terms of Service now explicitly outline the rules and obligations for these developers.

Lastly, the dispute-resolution provisions have been revised. This includes provisions related to resolving disputes between users, Quora/Poe, and third-party services. These changes aren't necessarily harmful, but they may be more complex and nuanced than before.

One new clause to be aware of in general is that the Terms of Service allow for binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court). While this is not explicitly flagged as a 'harmful' change, it may not be ideal for everyone, as it means you may have to participate in private hearings instead of going to court.

It's essential to note that the Terms of Service do not address potential harm or negative consequences. Their primary purpose is to clarify the rules and obligations of using Quora and Poe.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The arbitration process is now mandatory, whereas it was previously governed by general legal procedures.
- The dispute-notice window has been shortened.
- Class-action rights are now limited, whereas they were not previously waived in this version.
- A 30-day window has been added to opt-out of the new arbitration terms.
- The effective date of the document update is now tied to an event (the October 2023 data breach), whereas it was previously only mentioned as the date of a previous version.
- The terms now specifically update after a data breach, rather than prior to it.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes.

One of the main changes is related to arbitration. Previously, the Terms of Service left disputes to be governed by general legal procedures. However, the new version introduces a mandatory-arbitration clause. This means that if you have a dispute with us, you'll have to use this private dispute process (binding arbitration) instead of going to court.

Another key change is the shortening of the dispute-notice window. Previously, you had a longer period to notify us before entering into a dispute. Now, that window has been shortened.

Additionally, class-action rights have been limited. In the previous version, class actions were not specifically waived. Now, they are restricted.

A new clause has been added for opt-out. You now have a 30-day window to opt out of the new arbitration terms if you don't agree with them.

Lastly, the effective date of the document update is now tied to a specific event (the October 2023 data breach). This is different from the previous version.

As for clauses that may harm you:

* Mandatory arbitration could potentially limit your legal recourse in case of a dispute.
* The shortened dispute-notice window may make it harder for you to resolve issues with us quickly.
* Limited class-action rights might reduce the effectiveness of group actions against us, if needed.
* The new opt-out clause gives you 30 days to choose not to be subject to the new arbitration terms (should you object), but it doesn't change the fact that arbitration is now mandatory for those who stay.

The Terms of Service do not address the specific implications of the October 2023 data breach on this update.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated. Let's go over the changes.

**Default-private accounts for under-13 users**: Previously, standard account rules applied to users under 13. Now, these users have default-private accounts by default. This change might be beneficial for under-13 users, as it restricts who can interact with their accounts.

**Improved parental-consent flows**: The Terms of Service now require improved parental-consent flows for users under 13. This means that parents will need to provide consent for their child's account to interact with others or access certain features. This change is likely intended to provide additional safeguards for young users.

**Revised ROBUX/DEVEX provisions**: The sections on ROBUX and DEVEX have been revised. According to the changes, revisions were made but the impact on you isn't specified. Be aware that your use of Robux or DEVEX might be affected.

**New rules for generative-AI tools**: The updated Terms of Service include new rules for **Studio Assistant** and avatar-creation generative-AI tools. These new rules restrict how these tools can be used, potentially limiting your ability to create content with these tools.

**Updated arbitration class-waiver section**: The arbitration section has been updated to better clarify the process. However, arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) now has a **class action waiver**, which means you will not be able to join a class-action lawsuit against the company.

The updated Terms of Service contain no explicit clauses that seem intentionally harmful, but rather aim to provide better protections and clarity for users.

This means that going forward, disputes will be resolved through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of going to court) instead of following the previous process. While not explicitly stated, we can infer that this change might have altered the scope of potential legal outcomes for users.

**AI-Generated Trip Summaries:** The new Terms of Service mention AI-generated trip summaries. This new language highlights that trip summaries may include information generated by artificial intelligence and discuss driver/rider safety features. This change might increase concern for data confidentiality or misuse of AI-generated content.

**Liability Limitations Expanded:** The revised Terms of Service have expanded liability limitations to include third-party services. This means that in cases involving third-party services, the liability (legal responsibility) will be extended beyond the standard limits. While this change might provide some protection to Uber in certain circumstances, it remains unclear how this will specifically affect users.

These changes aim to reflect Uber's evolving policies in response to regulatory decisions and advancements in technology. Nonetheless, as with any updated agreement, it's essential to evaluate these changes carefully to understand how they may impact you.

- The NEW version includes a binding Universal Code of Conduct (UCoC), while the OLD version did not.
- The NEW version has strengthened paid-contributions disclosure rules, whereas the OLD version had limited disclosure rules.
- The NEW version includes modernized account-security provisions, whereas the OLD version had pre-modernization provisions.
- The NEW version explicitly covers automated tools and AI-assisted edits, while the OLD version had no specific clause.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some significant changes. Let's go over what's new.

One major change is the addition of a binding Universal Code of Conduct (UCoC). This is a new policy that applies to all users. Note that this policy is binding, meaning that if you fail to comply with the UCoC, you may face consequences.

Another significant change is the strengthening of paid-contributions disclosure rules. This means that if you're making contributions and getting paid for them, you're now required to disclose this information more clearly. This is aimed at maintaining the integrity of the platform and preventing any potential harm to its reputation.

There's also a modernization of account-security provisions. This means that the rules around keeping your account secure have been updated to be more in line with modern best practices. For example, this might include clearer guidance on password management and two-factor authentication.

Lastly, the Terms of Service are now explicitly covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits. This means that you're expected to follow the community guidelines when using automated tools or AI to make edits. However, note that this clause doesn't explicitly warn against any potential harm caused by these tools.

It's worth noting that one new component, the UCoC, is binding.

To sum up, the changes to the Terms of Service include:
* A binding Universal Code of Conduct (UCoC)
* Strengthened paid-contributions disclosure rules
* Modernized account-security provisions
* Explicit coverage of automated tools and AI-assisted edits

5. CHANGES TO TERMS. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use after changes constitutes acceptance.
6. SUPPORT. We aim to respond to support tickets within 5 business days.

user_input: Does Steam still require disputes to go to arbitration?
response: No, Steam does not require disputes to go to arbitration. The updated version of the Steam Subscriber Agreement (effective 2024) says that disputes must be filed in court, subject to venue rules.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STEAM SUBSCRIBER AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Steam (Valve) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: September 26, 2024 update removed the mandatory arbitration / class-action waiver clauses entirely - Valve now requires disputes to be filed in court (subject to venue rules), reversing several years of arbitration-only language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Steam (Valve) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ .

In the past, 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers likely did not have ads, but now they do, except in certain circumstances like with user-submitted content.

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Disney+ and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective January 27, 2025 for new subscribers and March 24, 2025 for existing ones: streaming titles may now show ads even on 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers, expanded arbitration with mass-arbitration procedures following Disney's earlier 2024 Wrongful-Death-case controversy, and updated content-availability language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Disney+ to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.disneyplus.com/legal/subscriber-agreement . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://www.disneyplus.com/legal/subscriber-agreement .

user_input: How do I keep my right to sue 23andMe after the data breach?
response:
To keep your right to sue 23andMe after the data breach, the Terms of Service tell you to opt out within 30 days. However, you must write to 23andMe to do this. If you don't write to opt out, you'll be required to participate in binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) for any breach-related claims. 

To opt out, you should contact 23andMe's customer support at their website https://www.23andme.com/.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — 23ANDME TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with 23andMe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: After the October 2023 data breach, 23andMe updated its TOS to add a mandatory-arbitration clause and 30-day opt-out window, requiring users who didn't write to opt out to arbitrate any breach-related claims; also limited class-action rights and shortened the dispute-notice window.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by 23andMe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/ . The previous version is available at https://www.23andme.com/legal/terms-of-service/full-version/2.0/ .
ground_truth:

Under the Terms updated after the October 2023 data breach, you are automatically opted in to mandatory arbitration unless you affirmatively opt out within the 30-day window described in the Terms by sending the company a written notice of objection. If you don't opt out, class-action rights are limited and disputes go to arbitration.
[MUST MENTION]
- mandatory arbitration
- 30-day
- opt out
- written
